presentingComplaint: Two days of worsening breathlessness and wheeze with increased sputum but no fever
history: Known GOLD group D COPD (FEV1 42% predicted) on tiotropium and formoterol/budesonide. Ex-smoker, 45 pack-years, stopped 3 years ago. Over 48 hours has developed increasing dyspnoea from baseline, audible wheeze and a modest rise in sputum volume that remains mucoid (clear/grey), not purulent. No fever, rigors, pleuritic pain or haemoptysis. Symptoms began the day after a cold-front cold snap and heavy exposure to household smoke; no sick contacts. Two prior exacerbations in the past year. No recent hospitalisation or antibiotics.
examination: Alert, mildly distressed, using accessory muscles, speaking in short sentences. Prolonged expiratory phase with diffuse polyphonic wheeze and reduced air entry bilaterally; no focal crepitations, no bronchial breathing, no consolidation. No calf tenderness or unilateral leg swelling. Mild ankle oedema chronic. No cyanosis at rest on 2L O2.

labs.ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO2 6.5 kPa, PaO2 8.1 kPa on 2L, HCO3 27 mmol/L

imaging: Chest X-ray: hyperinflated lung fields, flattened diaphragms, no focal consolidation, no effusion, no pneumothorax. No radiographic infiltrate to suggest pneumonia.
microbiology: Sputum mucoid; Gram stain unremarkable, culture pending but low pretest suspicion. Blood cultures not indicated (afebrile).
citations: GOLD Global Strategy for Prevention, Diagnosis and Management of COPD 2024
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective. No purulent sputum, afebrile, normal WBC/CRP and low procalcitonin argue against bacterial infection; per GOLD, antibiotics are reserved for increased sputum purulence plus increased volume/dyspnoea (2 of 3 Anthonisen criteria including purulence) or ventilatory support. Treat with controlled oxygen (target SpO2 88-92%), inhaled short-acting bronchodilators (salbutamol + ipratropium) and a short course of oral prednisolone 40 mg for 5 days.
contraindications: Avoid high-flow uncontrolled oxygen — risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure in chronic CO2 retainer
Systemic corticosteroid caution if diabetic (monitor glucose)
edgeCases: Purulent sputum or a rise in CRP/procalcitonin would reclassify as infective and justify antibiotics
Sudden severe pleuritic dyspnoea with normal CXR should prompt CTPA to exclude PE, a common COPD mimic/precipitant
Rising PaCO2 with falling pH (respiratory acidosis) mandates consideration of NIV
expectedMaiK: Classic non-infective COPD exacerbation: increased dyspnoea and wheeze with mucoid (non-purulent) sputum, afebrile, and normal inflammatory markers, so antibiotics are not indicated. Manage with controlled oxygen to 88-92%, intensified bronchodilators and a 5-day oral corticosteroid course, and reassess for hypercapnic respiratory failure.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the sputum purulent (colour change) or has its volume increased?
Any orthopnoea, PND or leg swelling to suggest heart failure as the cause?
expectedInvestigations: Arterial blood gas to assess for hypercapnia/respiratory acidosis
Chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax and effusion

crossAccept.rationale: COPD and asthma exacerbation share acute obstructive-airway management (bronchodilators + steroids).

regressionAssertions: stewardship tier must be null (non-infective — no antibiotics)
